You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE conductor (
    Conductor_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Age INT,
    Nationality TEXT,
    Year_of_Work INT,
    UNIQUE (Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE orchestra (
    Orchestra_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra TEXT,
    Conductor_ID INT,
    Record_Company TEXT,
    Year_of_Founded REAL,
    Major_Record_Format TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Orchestra_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Conductor_ID) REFERENCES conductor(Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE performance (
    Performance_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra_ID INT,
    Type TEXT,
    Date TEXT,
    Official_ratings_(millions) REAL,
    Weekly_rank TEXT,
    Share TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Performance_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Orchestra_ID) REFERENCES orchestra(Orchestra_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE show (
    Show_ID INT,
    Performance_ID INT,
    If_first_show bool,
    Result TEXT,
    Attendance REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (Performance_ID) REFERENCES performance(Performance_ID)
);

There isn’t a “famous” flag/column in this schema, so you’ll need to define what you mean by “famous.” Common ways to approximate it with your tables:

**1) Conductors with the most performances (most active/visible)**
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  COUNT(p.Performance_ID) AS performance_count
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY performance_count DESC;
```

**2) Conductors with the highest total audience (sum of attendance across shows)**
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  SUM(s.Attendance) AS total_attendance
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o   ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
JOIN show s        ON s.Performance_ID = p.Performance_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY total_attendance DESC;
```

**3) Conductors with the highest average official ratings**
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  AVG(p."Official_ratings_(millions)") AS avg_official_ratings_millions
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY avg_official_ratings_millions DESC;
```

Tell me which definition you want (or a different one), and how many “famous conductors” you want returned (e.g., top 5, top 10).
I want names of conductors who meet these criteria.

Which criteria do you mean—(1) most performances, (2) highest total attendance, or (3) highest average official ratings? Also, what cutoff should I use (e.g., top 10, or above a certain threshold)?

In the meantime, here are **name-only** versions for each option:

**1) Names of conductors with most performances (top 10)**
```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

**2) Names of conductors with highest total attendance (top 10)**
```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
JOIN show s ON s.Performance_ID = p.Performance_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY SUM(s.Attendance) DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

**3) Names of conductors with highest avg official ratings (top 10)**
```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY AVG(p."Official_ratings_(millions)") DESC
LIMIT 10;
```
I want names of conductors that have conducted multiple orchestras, not just one.

```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1;
```
I want to consider only conductors based on their past conducting activities.

If you want “multiple orchestras” based only on **past conducting activities**, we should count only orchestras that have at least one **performance** recorded.

```sql
SELECT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o   ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.Orchestra_ID) > 1;
```

If you also want to treat “past” as **before a certain date**, tell me the cutoff date and I’ll add `WHERE p.Date < ...`.
